subtopic: Deciding whether to quit or persist
subtype: Approach: find out what exactly is wrong using five whys [Thinking]
passage:
Ritu, you asked how I knew what I actually wanted. Honestly, I did a thing called five whys. I started with, why do I hate this job? Because Mondays feel heavy. Why? Because I do the same tasks every day. Why? Because nobody has given me anything new. Why? Because my role was never clearly defined. And why is that? Because I never asked, and my manager assumed I was fine.

I'm Chinmay, and I'd been ready to blame the salary. But the salary wasn't it. It was that I wasn't learning and didn't know what I was responsible for. That changed what I asked for: a clearer role and a project with something new in it, not just more money.

qa.q: What method did Chinmay use to find what was wrong?
What was Chinmay feeling about the job when the five whys began, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Chinmay felt heavy and stuck, shown by the dread of Mondays and the readiness to blame the salary.

qa.q: What could Chinmay do next with this answer, and why?
qa.a: Chinmay could take the two points to the manager and ask for a specific new project, because a problem named clearly is easier to fix than a general unhappiness.

qa.q: How might Ritu, who asked the question, see Chinmay's method?
qa.a: Ritu may see a simple method others could copy, and the answer shows a change from blaming pay to naming the real cause.

grounding: The person asks why the job feels bad repeatedly and finds a lack of learning and an unclear role, not the pay, is the real problem.

I'm Mridul, and Karthik and I share a flat in Pune. For weeks he came home from his first job and sat with his shoes still on, saying, "I hate it."
One Saturday he grabbed a notepad and asked himself out loud. "Why do I hate it? The work's boring. Why is it boring? I do the same reports every day. Why the same reports? Because nobody's told me what my role actually is. Why not? Because my manager thinks I'll figure it out. Why does that bother me? Because I'm not learning anything."
He looked up. "I always said it was the pay. It's not the pay."
He crossed out 'ask for raise' on his list and wrote 'ask for a clear role and one new skill by June'.
On Monday he left early for his manager's one-to-one. I don't know how it went inside, but he took his shoes off that evening.

qa.q: What did Karthik cross out on his list?
How does Karthik feel when he realises it is not the pay?
qa.a: He seems surprised and a little relieved, looking up to say it is not the pay after all.

qa.q: What else could Karthik do if the manager can't give a clearer role?
qa.a: He could look for roles that promise structured learning, since the five whys showed learning matters more to him than pay.

qa.q: How does the change look to Mridul?
qa.a: Mridul notices Karthik stops sitting with his shoes on, though Mridul can't know how the one-to-one went inside.

grounding: Shows the person asking why the job feels bad again and again and finding the root cause is lack of learning and an unclear role, not pay.

subtopic: Deciding whether to quit or persist
subtype: Approach: find out what exactly is wrong using five whys [Thinking]
passage:
Week one. Tarun came back from the bank branch every evening and told his sister Lakshmi he wanted to resign. "It's the salary," he said. "It's too low."
Week two. Lakshmi asked him to try something before deciding. On a Sunday he sat with a notebook and asked why, over and over. Why does the job feel bad? Because I dread going. Why? Because I don't know what I'm supposed to be good at. Why? Because I'm moved between counters with no training. Why? Nobody set goals for my role. And why does that bother me most? Because I'm not learning. He stared at it. "The salary isn't even on this page."
Week four. He asked his branch manager for a written role and a month on the loans desk with a senior. His pay stayed the same, but he stopped talking about resigning at dinner.

qa.q: Where did Tarun ask to spend a month?
qa.a: He asked for a month on the loans desk with a senior.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling when he stared at his notebook?
qa.a: He was surprised and a little unsettled, realising the salary he complained about did not appear in his answers at all.

qa.q: What else could Tarun try if the branch manager says no?
qa.a: He could look for a role elsewhere that offers clear training, since he now knows learning, not pay, is what he needs.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi see the change by week four?
qa.a: Lakshmi, who asked him to test his reasons, would likely feel relieved that dinner talk has moved away from resigning.

grounding: Shows the person asking why repeatedly about a bad job and finding the real problem is lack of learning and an unclear role, not pay.
